notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Deuteronomy 28:24–45, drawn from the pages I was able to access. (My search and fetch limits ran out, so some denominational and scholarly perspectives could not be retrieved; I indicate those gaps below.)

---

## Overview of the Passage (vv. 24–45)

The traditional reading sees these verses as the second, third, and part of the fourth series of curses within the larger curse section (vv. 15–68). Barnes divides the curses into five series: vv. 20–26 (first series: disease, famine, defeat); vv. 27–37 (second series: judgments on body, mind, and outward circumstances); vv. 38–48 (third series: affecting every kind of labour and enterprise); vv. 49–58 (fourth: siege horrors); vv. 58–68 (fifth: exile and dispersion).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Barnes' Notes)

The Cambridge Bible notes that the curse section is far more elaborated than the blessings, and the curses affecting the land and people while still in possession of it were intended to build a vivid impression by presenting picture after picture.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 24 — "The LORD will turn the rain of your land into dust and powder…"

**Traditional reading:** Instead of life-giving rain, God would send dust storms. Gill explains that through drought the soil would be dried and parched, its clods crumbled into dust, and then raised by winds into the air and let down again in destructive showers of dust. The Targum of Jonathan interprets it of the Lord sending a wind that raises dust upon the herbs of the fields.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Gill's Exposition)

Ellicott notes that the great desert lying on the eastern frontier of Palestine makes this "only too possible."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-24.htm (Ellicott)

The Cambridge Bible describes the sirocco (*Sherḳiyeh*) as bringing up "a fog of dust as dense and fine as a sea-mist, but very destructive."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan) adds that whole caravans have been buried under showers of sand, and the fine sand particles cause ophthalmia (eye inflammation) in Egypt.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Clarke's Commentary)

Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic) simply notes: a covenant-disobedient Israel would be cursed by the weather; the sky would not bring the rain essential to agriculture, bringing famine and starvation.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 25 — "The LORD will cause you to be defeated before your enemies…flee seven ways…object of horror to all kingdoms"

**Traditional reading:** The exact opposite of the blessing in v. 7. Ellicott notes the LXX uses *διασπορά* ("dispersion") here — the very word used for the dispersed Israelites in the NT (John 7:35; 1 Peter 1:1). The threat is repeated in Jeremiah 15:4 for the sins of King Manasseh.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-25.htm (Ellicott)

Gill says this was fulfilled at various times — by Philistines, Assyrians, Babylonians, and Romans — but was "exactly fulfilled at their last destruction by the Romans, when they were sent by them into various countries, and have been ever since scattered about in each of the nations of the world."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-25.htm (Gill)

Keil & Delitzsch: Israel would become *לזעוה* — "a moving to and fro," i.e., "a ball for all the kingdoms of the earth to play with."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-25.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)

Barnes distinguishes this from Leviticus 26:33: here it means being "tossed to and fro at the will of others, driven from one country to another without any certain settlement," not simply dispersed among pagan nations.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-25.htm (Barnes)

---

### v. 26 — "Your corpses will be food for all the birds of the air and beasts of the earth, with no one to scare them away."

**Traditional reading:** The greatest ignominy for the dead — being left unburied. This is a frequent threat against the ungodly (cf. 1 Kings 14:11; Psalm 79:2; Jeremiah 7:33; 16:4).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-25.htm (Keil & Delitzsch, Pulpit Commentary notes)

Guzik summarises: God would not fight for them, and their dead would be devoured by birds and beasts.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 27 — "The LORD will afflict you with the boils of Egypt, with tumors and scabs and itch…"

**Traditional reading:** Barnes identifies the "botch" (KJV) as boils (see Exodus 9:9), the "emerods" as tumors (as the Philistines suffered in 1 Samuel 5:6, 9), and the "scab" and "itch" as representing various loathsome skin diseases common in Syria and Egypt.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Barnes' Notes)

Guzik notes that the Hebrew word *opel* for "tumors" means "a swelling" and is usually thought to refer to hemorrhoids, tumors, bubonic plague, or leprosy (citing Kalland).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 28 — "The LORD will afflict you with madness, blindness, and confusion of mind"

**Traditional reading:** Mental maladies added to the bodily plagues. Barnes holds that "blindness" here is most probably *mental* blindness (cf. Lamentations 4:14; Zephaniah 1:17; 2 Corinthians 3:14ff).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Barnes' Notes)

Matthew Henry: "Those who walk by sight, and not by faith, are in danger of losing reason itself, when everything about them looks frightful."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-24.htm (Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary)

---

### v. 29 — "At noon you will grope about like a blind man in the darkness…"

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott notes this is the exact opposite of the promise to Joshua (Deuteronomy 1:8 — "thou shalt have good success"). He cross-references Isaiah 29:10–14: when men can no longer follow God's word, "the wisdom of their wise men shall perish."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/28.htm

Guzik: This belongs to the series of mental and physical afflictions that reduce the sufferers to powerlessness before their enemies.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 30 — "You will be pledged in marriage to a woman, but another man will violate her…build a house but will not live in it…plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit."

**Traditional reading:** Repeated, terrible injustices — the reversal of covenant blessings. Barnes notes the marginal references show fulfilment throughout Israel's history. Clarke: "Perhaps no people under the sun have been more oppressed and spoiled than the rebellious Jews. Indeed, this has been their portion, with but little intermission, for nearly 1,800 years."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/ (Guzik, citing Clarke)

---

### v. 31 — "Your ox will be slaughtered before your eyes, but you will not eat any of it…"

**Traditional reading:** Part of the same series of injustices. The point is the utter helplessness of the disobedient covenant people: they watch their own property taken or destroyed and can do nothing.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 32 — "Your sons and daughters will be given to another nation, while your eyes grow weary looking for them…"

**Traditional reading:** Clarke notes a specific historical fulfilment: "In several countries, particularly in Spain and Portugal, the children of the Jews have been taken from them by order of government, and educated in the Popish faith."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/ (Guzik, citing Clarke)

The Cambridge Bible observes that this captivity in v. 32 is only partial — Israel itself is still at home lamenting it.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

---

### v. 33 — "A people you do not know will eat the produce of your land…"

**Traditional reading:** Foreign invaders consume everything the Israelites have laboured for. Part of the reversal of the blessing in v. 12a (where the Lord would "open His good treasure, the heavens, to give rain…and bless all the work of your hand").
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

---

### v. 34 — "You will be driven mad by the sights you see."

**Traditional reading:** The cumulative effect of all the preceding horrors — the psychological devastation of watching everything collapse. Guzik: "All these tragedies would bring a dreadful result: Israel would be driven mad because of the sight which your eyes see."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 35 — "The LORD will afflict you with painful, incurable boils on your knees and thighs, from the soles of your feet to the top of your head."

**Traditional reading:** The Cambridge Bible notes this verse may be a later intrusion or displacement, since it seems to interrupt the narrative flow (the disease theme is resumed from v. 27 rather abruptly).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

Guzik: The affliction covers the entire body — "from the sole of your foot to the top of your head" — indicating total, inescapable suffering.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 36 — "The LORD will bring you and the king you appoint to a nation neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you will worship other gods…"

**Traditional reading:** This is the first explicit threat of national exile (the king and the people together). The Cambridge Bible notes this is a turning point: after the exile of nation and king is foretold, vv. 38ff return to describe aggravated conditions while still in the land.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

Guzik: This was fulfilled in the Babylonian captivity (King Jehoiachin and others exiled) and later under Rome. The irony is severe: Israel, who was to worship Yahweh alone, would be forced in exile to serve "gods of wood and stone."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 37 — "You will become an object of horror, scorn, and ridicule among all the nations…"

**Traditional reading:** This is the reversal of v. 10 ("all peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD, and they shall be afraid of you"). Instead of being feared for God's blessing, they become a byword and object of derision.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

---

### vv. 38–42 — Agricultural and family ruin (locusts, worms, dropping olives, captivity)

**Traditional reading:** Barnes places these in the third series of judgments "affecting every kind of labour and enterprise until it had accomplished the total ruin of the nation."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Barnes' Notes)

- **v. 38:** "Sow much seed…harvest little, because the locusts will consume it." The reversal of agricultural blessing.
- **v. 39:** "Plant vineyards…neither drink the wine nor gather the grapes, because worms will eat them." Barnes identifies the "worms" as the vine-weevil, against which naturalists prescribed elaborate precautions.
- **v. 40:** Olive trees throughout the territory, but the olives "drop off" (or, some render, "shall be plundered").
- **v. 41:** Sons and daughters go into captivity. The Cambridge Bible notes this repeats the theme from v. 32, possibly indicating a later expansion or the discursive style of Deuteronomy.
- **v. 42:** Locusts ("the cricket" in some translations) consume all trees and produce — total agricultural devastation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Barnes)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### vv. 43–44 — "The foreigner living among you will rise higher and higher…He will lend to you, but you will not lend to him. He will be the head, and you will be the tail."

**Traditional reading:** The complete reversal of the blessing in vv. 12–13, where Israel was promised they would "lend to many nations but not borrow" and be "the head and not the tail." Barnes: "Contrast Deuteronomy 28:12 and Deuteronomy 28:13."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Barnes' Notes)

Guzik: This describes the role reversal of Israelites and resident aliens (sojourners). The foreigner who was supposed to be under Israel's benevolent rule now dominates them.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

---

### v. 45 — "All these curses will come upon you. They will pursue you and overtake you until you are destroyed, since you did not obey the LORD your God…"

**Traditional reading:** This verse returns to the keynote of the whole curse section (cp. v. 15) and forms an obvious conclusion to the curses, which "may originally have closed here."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

Ellicott stresses that "till thou be destroyed" does *not* mean exterminated. The Hebrew root is connected with "smiting" — the idea is "to crush" (cf. 2 Kings 13:7: "the king of Syria had destroyed them, and had made them like the dust by threshing").
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/28.htm (from earlier fetch)

Calvin (as summarised on StudyLight): "He not only confirms what he has already said, but takes away all hope of alleviation, since God's scourges shall not cease until they have repented… The ungodly by their subterfuges only bring it to pass that they accumulate upon themselves heavier punishments, which will never cease to afflict them until they are destroyed by them."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-45.html (Calvin's commentary summary)

Benson (Methodist): Some critics divide the prophecies — the preceding part relating to the former captivity under the Chaldeans, and the remainder to the latter captivity under the Romans. But Bishop Newton argued no such division was intended; the prophecies "have all been more amply fulfilling during the latter period." Benson adds: "Their destruction by the Romans, far more dreadful than the former, shows that their sin in rejecting Christ was more provoking to God than idolatry itself."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-45.html (Benson Commentary)

Keil & Delitzsch: The curses were "for a sign and for a wonder" (v. 46) because their magnitude manifested the supernatural interposition of God. "For ever" applies to the generation smitten, but does not involve "the perpetual rejection of the whole nation, or the impossibility of the conversion and restoration of a remnant" (cf. Isaiah 10:22; 6:13; Romans 9:27; 11:5).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-45.html (Keil & Delitzsch)

---

## Denominational Distinctives

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The Reformed tradition reads Deuteronomy 28 within covenant theology: these curses are the sanctions of the Mosaic covenant. Ligonier teaches that the blessings and curses are "largely 'physical' in nature, but not exclusively so, for both typify spiritual realities." The ultimate covenant curse is exile — banishment from God's saving presence, which was felt most powerfully within the borders of the Promised Land. Crucially, Christ is the sinless substitute whose perfect obedience allows believers to enjoy eternal blessings; trusting Him alone is "the only way to escape the ultimate exile from God's saving presence."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/curse-god

The Gospel Coalition notes that covenant theology explains the law/gospel distinction within these chapters: the law drives us to Christ, who bore the covenant curse (Galatians 3:10–14).
— https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/covenant-theology/

### Baptist
Spurgeon, cited by the Gospel Coalition, held that "the doctrine of the covenant lies at the root of all true theology," indicating Baptist covenant theologians substantially agree with the Reformed reading of these curses as Mosaic covenant sanctions.
— https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/covenant-theology/

*(I was unable to retrieve specific Baptist verse-by-verse material from desiringgod.org, spurgeon.org, or gty.org for these verses within my search limits.)*

### Methodist / Wesleyan
Clarke's Commentary (Methodist) emphasises the historical fulfilment of these curses in the suffering of the Jewish people through centuries, especially noting the forced conversion of Jewish children in Catholic countries and the Roman destruction. Wesley's Notes (as referenced on StudyLight) summarise v. 24 tersely: "Either thy rain shall be as unprofitable…or instead of rain shall come nothing but dust."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Clarke, Wesley's Notes)

Benson reads the curses as fulfilled both in the Babylonian and Roman captivities, with the Roman destruction being the more severe because of the greater sin of rejecting Christ.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-45.html (Benson)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
David Guzik (Enduring Word) reads these curses as literal historical realities fulfilled from the Old Testament period through the Roman siege of Jerusalem and beyond. He emphasises that despite the horrifying reality of these curses in history, "God is not finished with Israel — Ezekiel 37 promises a national revival, and the curses will not be their final legacy." He also notes the church's centuries of persecution of the Jewish people as a sobering warning that God promised to curse those who curse Abraham's descendants (Genesis 12:3).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges (a critical, pre-exilic dating perspective) suggests that vv. 26–37 and v. 41 may be later expansions because they elaborate beyond what the blessings section contained. However, it also argues that the entire discourse "may well be pre-exilic" since there is no promise of restoration for the exiled penitent people (contrast Deuteronomy 4:20–40, which is taken as evidence of an exilic date). The discursive, repetitive style of D makes it "impossible to say whether some even of those vv. are original or expansions."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/28.htm

The NET Bible translation notes were referenced in my search results only as a parallel text without study notes being displayed.
— https://biblehub.com/net/deuteronomy/28.htm

*(bibleodyssey.org was not reachable within search limits.)*

## Summary of Key Observations

1. **These verses are part of an ancient treaty form**: The curses correspond structurally to the blessings (vv. 3–14) and follow the pattern of ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaties where curses were typically longer and more detailed than blessings, to stress the seriousness of covenant violation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/28-24.html (Constable, Barnes)

2. **Historical fulfilment is widely attested**: All the traditional commentators (Gill, Clarke, Benson, Barnes, Guzik) point to fulfilments in the Assyrian, Babylonian, and Roman periods, with the Roman destruction (AD 70) seen as the fullest and most terrifying realisation.

3. **"Destroyed" does not mean annihilated**: Ellicott is explicit that the Hebrew root means "to crush" or "smite," consistent with Israel's continued existence as a scattered but preserved people (v. 46ff).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/28.htm

4. **Christologically, the curses point to the cross**: The Reformed tradition emphasises that Christ bore the covenant curse on behalf of His people (Galatians 3:13), making Deuteronomy 28 not merely a historical threat to Israel but part of the redemptive-historical framework pointing to the gospel.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/curse-god
